units.Habakkuk 3:14: Thou didst cut the heads of rulers in bewilderment; they will be shaken in it. They will open their bridles like a poor person eating secretly.
units.Habakkuk 3:3: God will come from Teman, the Holy One from a mountain shaded and thickly wooded. Diapsalma. His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of His praise.
units.Habakkuk 3:4: His brightness will be like light; horns are in His hands, and He established mighty love of His strength.
units.Habakkuk 3:6: He stood, and the earth shook; He looked, and nations melted. Mountains were crushed violently; everlasting hills melted.
units.Wisdom of Solomon 18:14: For while quiet silence surrounded all things and night was midway through its swift course,

units.Habakkuk 3:12: With threat Thou wilt diminish the earth, and in fury Thou wilt bring nations down.
units.Habakkuk 3:13: Thou didst go out for Thy people’s salvation, to save Thine anointed ones. Thou didst cast death upon the heads of lawless people and didst raise bonds up to the neck. Diapsalma.
units.Habakkuk 3:15: Thou didst drive Thy horses into the sea as they troubled much water.
units.Psalms 109:4: The Lord swore and will not change His purpose: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.
units.Psalms 109:5: The Lord at your right hand crushed kings on the day of His anger.

reread_versions.relationship: Personification: a moving word in divine intervention
reread_versions.rationale: Habakkuk places a word going before God as He goes out with His feet in sandals. Wisdom portrays God's all-powerful word leaping from heaven as a warrior into the doomed land and standing upon the earth. Both give a word movement within a scene of divine intervention. Habakkuk does not call its word a warrior or a sword, and the sandals belong to the One going out rather than being transferred to Wisdom's personified word.
reread_versions.source_text: A word will go before Him, and He will go out, His feet in sandals.

target_units.text: Thine all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from royal thrones, a stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land, carrying Thine unfeigned command as a sharp sword;
standing there, it filled all things with death; it touched heaven while standing upon the earth.

reread_versions.relationship: Divine-war imagery: rulers and heads struck down
reread_versions.rationale: Habakkuk addresses God as cutting rulers' heads in bewilderment during the saving intervention described nearby. The psalm says the Lord crushes kings in anger and crushes heads while judging the nations. Both depict divine victory over ruling power through blows to heads. The psalm does not explain Habakkuk's ensuing bridles and secretly eating poor person, and those native clauses are not replaced with another battle description.
